extracted.intended_audience: authors/writers seeking developmental editing for book manuscripts (fiction and nonfiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what to expect from a developmental edit for book-length manuscripts, including readiness, scope of feedback, deliverables, timeline, cost, and how to choose an editor. Applies to both fiction (immersion, character, plot) and nonfiction (logical flow, engagement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Readiness for a developmental edit
rubrics_metrics.description: The developmental edit is usually the very first type of edit you need when embarking on your writing journey. I usually prefer to work with authors after they have finished their manuscript and have reviewed it themselves at least once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give yourself a little vacation and then go back with fresh eyes; finishing a full draft first helps avoid an endless revision loop or quitting after early feedback. Exception: some authors need help earlier and may work with book coaches who provide staged feedback during drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro-level manuscript evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: I look at the manuscript from a macro level, evaluating each of the different story or narrative elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For fiction, consider how to make the story more immersive. For nonfiction, ensure the information flows logically and stays engaging. The focus is on structure and overarching elements rather than sentence-level polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book coaching / working during drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Some developmental editors (also known as book coaches) will work with authors through the entire writing process—giving feedback on a few chapters at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach supports building out initial concepts or completing a first draft but may increase risk of getting stuck in revision loops; weigh the benefit of earlier support against the value of finishing a full draft first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing the right developmental editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for someone with the right skill set, appropriate training, and familiarity with your subject matter and/or genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also consider compatible working styles (phone/virtual meetings vs email-only), whether the editor offers discovery calls, and how often they check in during a project. There is no single correct style—think about what you need for a successful working relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample edits: scope and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors often do a sample edit as a way to evaluate the state of the writing and how long it will take to do the full edit. But this method works much better for line or copy editing because they are concrete and focused on sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developmental suggestions are more conceptual and made with the context of the entire manuscript. In sample edits, expect evaluation of a few chapters with general notes and the caveat that the editor's opinion might change after reading the whole book. Use the sample to discuss story, goals, and working style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issues a developmental edit should identify
rubrics_metrics.description: The developmental edit evaluates the structure and elements of a manuscript to see what is working well and what is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical problems to catch include sagging middles, inconsistent characters, jumpy timelines, and unbelievable plot elements. The goal is to revise the story so it is an engaging journey from beginning to end and keeps readers coming back.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback format and deliverables
rubrics_metrics.description: I use comments and tracked changes in the manuscript and a separate editorial letter to give you in-depth feedback and an analysis of your manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editorial letter points out specific instances where things are working, where they might be further developed, makes small editorial suggestions, and summarizes overall impressions. Letters typically run 10 to 30 pages and cover each relevant element. A follow-up virtual meeting is often offered to answer questions and brainstorm solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeline, rounds, and revision expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Once I start a developmental edit project, it takes about three to six weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors normally quote and schedule one round of developmental editing at a time. Because developmental edits can result in substantial revisions, editors may avoid strict timelines and are often willing to do a second evaluation or additional round before moving into line/copy editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost determinants and pricing benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost and overall timeline can vary quite a bit depending on the length and complexity of the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get a personalized quote; rates often align with the Editorial Freelancers Association’s posted averages. Expect pricing to scale with manuscript length, complexity, and level of editorial support requested.
